spec.name: Lantern Lander Mk2
spec.tagline: A flat cardboard canopy slows the fall to a third of free-fall speed; paper cups on all six faces crush on landing; the egg rides in a sponge pocket at the centre.
spec.summary: The device is a 27 × 27 × 27.2 cm lantern. On top, a 27 cm square of corrugated cardboard with a vent hole acts as a drag plate: the device weighs only about 300 g, so it settles at about 7.8 m/s instead of the 22 m/s it would reach with no air, and the low-hanging mass keeps it falling canopy-up like a shuttlecock. Under the canopy hangs a 16 × 16 × 12 cm cardboard sleeve. Four 9 oz paper cups under the floor are the main crumple zone; four 3 oz cups on the canopy cover an upside-down landing; sixteen 3 oz cups on the four walls cover side, edge and corner landings. Every inner face of the sleeve is lined with a 2 cm folded-newspaper pad. At the centre, the egg lies in a pocket traced into a kitchen sponge inside an egg-carton pod, which sits in a cardboard socket glued to the floor pad and is held by two rubber bands, so it goes back to exactly the same spot after every test drop. A door in the front wall lets the pod out in under a minute. Crushed cups and pads are swapped from a bag of pre-cut spares.
why_this_design: Drag first: a 27 cm canopy on a 300 g device gives a terminal velocity near 7.8 m/s, reached before the 3rd floor, so the 25 m drop lands no harder than a 10 m drop.
Stable on the way down: the canopy is the centre of pressure and the sleeve, cups and egg hang 10 cm below it, so any tilt swings back canopy-up. The vent stops the plate rocking.
Crush on every face: cups under the floor, on the canopy and on all four walls mean a tumble or a wall clip still lands on 4 to 7 cm of paper cup, then a 2 cm pad, then the sponge.

No free flight inside: the egg pod sits in a socket on the floor pad instead of hanging on slack bands, so it decelerates with the frame and never hits a wall at full speed. The panel's physics judge found this flaw in every hammock design.

Cheap and repeatable: one cardboard box, two bags of paper cups, a sponge, an egg carton and rubber bands, about $5. The pocket, the socket and marker marks put the egg back in the same place; cups and pads swap from spares between drops.

egg_access.open: Pull the band off the door tab and swing the door down on its tape hinge. Hook a finger under the two retaining bands and slip them off their toggles on the far wall. Slide the pod out through the door by its tab.
egg_access.seat: Open the pod lid. Lift the egg out by the narrow end, check it and dry it. Put the egg back wide end down into the traced pocket with the pencil N mark on the shell against the N on the sponge. Close the lid, push the pod back through the door until it drops into the socket ring with its UP arrow in line with the marker line on the floor pad.
egg_access.close: Hook the two retaining bands back onto their toggles (numbered 1 and 2), swing the door up and loop the latch band over its tab. Look through the vent: the lid should be flat and centred.
egg_access.same_place_feature: Three things fix the position: the egg can only sit one way in the pocket cut to its outline, the pod can only drop into the socket ring, and the UP arrow on the pod meets the line on the floor pad.

reset_between_drops: Carry the device to the inspection table. Open the door and take the egg out before touching anything else; note whether it is intact.

Look at the four bottom cups: any cup shorter than 5 cm or split is swapped (peel the tape collar, twist the cup off its glue dab, hot-glue or tape a fresh cup on, re-tape the collar). Expect to swap all four after the 5th-floor and top drops.
Check the side and top cups: swap any that are dented more than 1 cm.
Press the floor pad and wall pads: swap any pad that stays below 1.5 cm thick.
Check the two retaining bands and the door band for nicks; replace from the bag if in doubt.
Look along the canopy: if an edge or corner is folded, splint it with a strip of tape on both sides.
Re-seat the egg (or a fresh test egg) in the pocket, pod into the socket, bands on, door latched.
Re-measure L, W, H and write the numbers on the drop log; climb to the next floor.

test_ladder.purpose: Proves the egg access, the socket and the cups work before anything is at risk: does it land canopy-up, do the bottom cups crush evenly?

build_steps.title: Cut the canopy
build_steps.detail: Mark a 27 × 27 cm square on flat, uncreased cardboard and cut it with the box cutter against the ruler in two passes. Find the centre by drawing both diagonals and cut a 3 cm hole there. Fold a strip of packing tape over all four edges. On the underside draw a 16 × 16 cm square centred on the hole.
build_steps.tip: Cut on a scrap board and keep the flutes running the same way on every panel.

build_steps.title: Cut and fold the sleeve
build_steps.detail: Cut one strip 64.8 × 12 cm (four 16 cm panels plus a 0.8 cm glue tab). Score the three fold lines lightly with the box cutter against the ruler, fold into a 16 × 16 cm square tube and hot-glue the tab inside. Cut a 15.2 × 15.2 cm floor and glue it flush into the bottom of the tube.
build_steps.tip: Score only the top liner of the board so the fold stays sharp without cracking.

build_steps.title: Cut the door
build_steps.detail: On one wall (this becomes the front), draw a 6 cm wide × 9 cm tall rectangle centred left-to-right with its bottom edge 1 cm above the floor. Cut the two sides and the bottom, leave the top as a hinge and run tape over the hinge. Glue a small cardboard tab to the outside bottom of the door and a matching tab on the wall below it for the latch band.
build_steps.tools: ruler, box cutter, tape, hot glue
build_steps.tip: The pod is 5.2 cm wide; test that it passes through before you glue anything else.

build_steps.title: Make the pads
build_steps.detail: Fold newspaper into two 12 × 12 cm pads and four 12 × 8 cm pads, each 2 cm thick (about 8 layers folded, then taped round the middle). Tape one square pad to the floor. Tape a rectangular pad to the inside of each wall, centred, 2 cm above the floor pad. Keep the second square pad for the canopy.
build_steps.tip: Fold the pads so the open edges face the wall: they crush more evenly.

build_steps.title: Make the pod and its socket
build_steps.detail: Cut one cell from the egg carton together with the lid section directly above it, keeping the hinge. Cut two 1 cm thick discs from the sponge to fit the cell. Stand the egg wide end down on one disc, trace round it with the marker and cut the pocket to half the disc thickness; write N at the narrow end. Glue that disc into the cell and the other disc inside the lid. Draw a big UP arrow on the outside of the lid. Cut a 1.2 × 20 cm cardboard strip, roll it into a ring the pod base just fits into, tape it, and hot-glue the ring to the centre of the floor pad. Draw a line across the floor pad that the UP arrow will meet.
build_steps.tip: Write N on the egg shell too with a pencil so the egg goes back the same way every time.

build_steps.title: Fit the retaining bands
build_steps.detail: Punch a hole with a pencil tip at the top centre of each wall, 1 cm below the top edge. Push a #33 band through the front hole from inside and slip a 3 cm straw toggle through the loop outside; stretch the band across the sleeve, over the socket, out through the back hole and onto a second toggle. Repeat left to right. Number the four toggles 1 to 4 so a swapped band always goes back to the same holes.
build_steps.tip: The bands should press the pod lid down firmly but still let you slip them off with one finger.

build_steps.title: Glue the canopy on
build_steps.detail: Tape the second square pad to the underside of the canopy inside the 16 cm square. Run hot glue along the top edges of the four walls, press the canopy on with the pad inside the sleeve, hold for a minute, then add a tape tab over the joint at each corner outside.
build_steps.tip: Check through the vent that the pad sits flat before the glue sets.

build_steps.title: Fit the bottom crumple cups
build_steps.detail: Hot-glue the base of a 9 oz cup under each corner of the floor, mouth down, with its centre 4 cm in from each edge, and wrap a collar of tape from cup to floor. The cup mouths are the only part that touches the ground.
build_steps.tip: Press each cup on a kitchen scale first: it should start to fold between 2 and 3 kg. A cup that folds much easier gets a second cup nested inside.

build_steps.title: Fit the top and side cups
build_steps.detail: Hot-glue four 3 oz cups base down on the four top corners of the canopy, 3.2 cm in from the edges, mouths up. Hot-glue four 3 oz cups on each wall with bases against the wall and mouths outward: two at 3 cm above the floor and two at 3 cm below the top, each 5.2 cm left and right of the wall centre, clear of the door. Tape collars round every cup base.
build_steps.tip: Squeeze each 3 oz cup gently to put four shallow vertical creases in it so it buckles instead of splitting.

build_steps.title: Load and check the envelope
build_steps.detail: Seat a test egg, close the pod, drop the pod into the socket with the UP arrow on the line, hook the bands, latch the door. Measure L and W across the canopy (27 cm) and H from the cup mouths on the floor to the top of the bumper cups (27.2 cm). Weigh if you can: about 305 g with the egg. Write the three numbers on the canopy.
build_steps.tip: Nothing may stick out past the canopy edge: the side cups end exactly at it.

build_steps.title: Pack the spares bag
build_steps.detail: Four 9 oz cups and twenty 3 oz cups (pre-creased), two folded pads, seven bands, the spare wall panel, tape, scissors, marker, the drop log sheet and the test eggs in their carton.
build_steps.tip: Pre-cut the tape collars and stick them to a plastic card so a cup swap takes two minutes.

build_steps.title: Bench test at home
build_steps.detail: Hold the device level by the canopy edges at shoulder height over a hard floor and let go. It should land on the four cups and stay upright. Open the door: the pod must still be in its socket with the arrow on the line. Then shake the device hard and check again.
build_steps.tip: If the pod moved, tighten the bands by looping them once more round their toggles.

drop_plan.site: The stairwell balcony or an open window on the drop side of the school building, with a hard, flat landing area below and nothing (cars, bushes, railings) within 4 m of the target.

roles.task: Carries the device up, loads the egg, checks the envelope, calls the sequence, releases level.
Stand at the keep-out line either side of the target, keep people out, call 'zone clear', watch the fall and call 'device down'.
Films the drop from outside the keep-out line and times release to landing (the model predicts about 3.9 s).
Waits outside the line, walks in only after 'device down', opens the door, takes the egg out and records the result and the cup damage on the log sheet.

sequence: Egg checker marks the target square on the ground directly under the release point and walks the keep-out circle; spotters take their places.
Dropper loads the egg, seats the pod, hooks the bands, latches the door, measures and writes the three dimensions on the log.
Dropper climbs to the floor for this drop and holds the device out over the rail, level, at arm's length, at least 1 m clear of the wall.
Spotters call 'zone clear'. Dropper calls 'dropping in 3, 2, 1' and opens both hands at the same time.
Everyone stays still until a spotter calls 'device down'. Then the egg checker goes in alone.
Reset per the between-drops procedure, log the result, and move up to the next floor of the ladder.
drop_plan.release_technique: Hold the canopy by two opposite edges with the fingertips, elbows straight, device level, cups down. Do not throw, lower or push: open both hands at the same instant so it leaves with no spin and no sideways speed.
drop_plan.orientation_at_release: Canopy up and level; the sleeve and cups hanging straight down; the door facing the building so the dropper can see the latch.
safety: Nobody inside the 4 m keep-out circle from the moment the dropper leans over the rail until 'device down'.
The dropper keeps both feet on the floor and leans only to the elbows; a second person holds the dropper's belt or shirt at the top floor.
No drop if the device swings in the hands at the rail: wait for the gust to pass.
Hard, flat landing area only: no grass (it hides results), no stairs, no parked cars.
Eggs are raw: the checker carries wipes and a bag for a broken one.
drop_plan.landing_zone: A 1.5 m square marked in chalk or tape on hard ground directly below the release point, inside a 4 m keep-out radius.

egg_prep: Use a large egg at room temperature; check it in the light for hairline cracks and reject any you find.
Write a small N in pencil on the narrow end and your initials on the wide end.
Dry the shell; a damp egg slips in the pocket.
Seat it wide end down in the traced pocket with the N against the N on the sponge, close the lid, band the pod.
Keep the final egg in its carton until drop 4; use the four test eggs for the ladder.
changes_from_panel: The judge panel ranked the Flat-Top Lantern Lander first on buildability and clarity but its physics judge found a fatal flaw shared by every hammock design: rubber bands are far too weak to slow a 100 g pod at 7 m/s, so the pod crosses its 'free travel' at full speed and hits a wall or pad. Mk2 therefore seats the pod in a socket on the floor pad, so the egg decelerates with the frame through the cups.

Cups now cover all six faces (4 × 9 oz below, 4 × 3 oz above, 16 × 3 oz on the walls) and every inner face carries a 2 cm pad, taking the omnidirectional idea from the Hex-Cage concept that scored best on physics.
The traced sponge pocket, the N mark and the UP arrow come from the Balloon-Cage concept's cradle, which the judges liked for putting the egg back in the same place.
The sleeve is 12 cm tall instead of 16: with no hammock there is nothing to hang, which saves mass and leaves room for 9.3 cm cups below and 5.5 cm cups above inside the 30 cm limit.
The balloon-pillow synthesis the panel produced was rejected by all of its own reviewers (pillows cannot carry the energy, build time over 3 h, egg access impossible as written) and is not used.
spec.worst_case_statement: The device may clip the wall and tumble onto a side, an edge, a corner or its top. Every face has its own cups, every inner face a pad, and the egg sits in a sponge pocket at the centre, so the model's peak load stays under the 90 g assumed for a cradled egg in every orientation, with the thinnest margin on a corner.
spec.cost_statement: Everything except the cups, a sponge and the eggs comes free from home: a cardboard box, newspaper, an egg carton, rubber bands, tape. A dollar store supplies two bags of paper cups and a sponge. Estimated total about $5.25 if nothing is at home, under $4 with eggs already in the fridge.

alternatives.name: Flat-Top Lantern Lander (rigid 27 cm drag canopy, 8-band egg hammock, swappable paper-cup crumple legs top and bottom)
alternatives.concept: A 27 x 27 cm flat corrugated-cardboard canopy with a 3 cm centre vent sits on top; a 16 x 16 x 16 cm open corrugated sleeve ('lantern') hangs under it, and inside the sleeve the egg rides in an egg-carton pod inside a sock, held mid-air by 8 rubber bands running to the 8 corners of the sleeve. Four pre-creased 3 oz paper cups glued under the sleeve are the primary crumple legs; four more on top of the canopy are the bumper for an inverted landing; the canopy edge and sleeve walls are the crumple path for side, edge and corner hits. Because almost all the mass hangs 10-12 cm below the canopy (centre of pressure), it falls canopy-up like a shuttlecock and reaches a terminal velocity of only about 7.4 m/s by roughly 10 m, so every drop from the 3rd floor upward hits at the same speed. The egg never touches cardboard from any direction: it has at least 3 cm of elastic travel vertically and 5 cm sideways before it reaches a newspaper backstop pad, and behind every pad there is a crumple cup or crushable cardboard. The pod comes out through a side door in under a minute and goes back against marker registration marks, and every sacrificial part (cups, bands, pads) is swapped from a bag of pre-cut spares.

alternatives.name: Shuttlecock Dart (nose-first cup-nest crumple, sling-held egg, fixed drag dish)
alternatives.concept: A 13 cm corrugated-cardboard cube ("core") holds the egg at its exact centre in a pantyhose sock pocket stretched between 8 rubber bands (4 to the top corners, 4 to the bottom corners), so the egg is positively located and cannot touch any wall; the inside of every wall carries its own soft cushion (egg-carton patches, a kitchen sponge on the floor). Under the core is a sacrificial nose made of 4 nested 8-oz paper cups (base down) that crush progressively over about 9 cm; on top is a removable "hat" (lid + a 27 cm diameter, 4 cm deep plastic-bag dish on paperboard spokes) that supplies most of the drag and, because it sits well above the centre of mass, keeps the device falling nose-first like a badminton shuttlecock. Every outside face and edge of the core wears its own paper-cup crumple pad, so a tumble, side, edge, corner or upside-down landing still has a crush path before anything reaches the inner cushions. With 312 g total and 0.057 m2 of drag area the device reaches terminal velocity (about 8.4 m/s) by the 3rd floor, so the egg sees roughly 30 g average / 39 g peak on the designed nose-first landing from 25 m instead of the 22 m/s no-drag case. The hat lifts off in 10 s, the egg comes out of the sock in 30 s and goes back to the same marked spot; the nose nest and pads are tape-mounted and swapped from a bag of pre-cut spares. Bill of materials is $2.75 to $6.60 depending on what is already at home.

alternatives.name: Hex-Cage: six-cup omnidirectional skewer cube
alternatives.concept: A 26.5 cm cube space frame of doubled bamboo skewers, skinned with grocery-bag film and braced by six packing-tape face diagonals (which form an inscribed tetrahedron, so the cube cannot shear). The raw egg sits at the exact geometric centre in a pantyhose toe-pocket held by eight pantyhose tethers to the eight corners, so the device has no 'up': whichever face, edge or corner hits first, the egg travels inward toward that side. Pointing at the egg from every face is an inverted, pre-crushed paper cup glued rim-down to a paperboard disc on the film; in a face-on landing the cup is backed by the ground itself and folds at a calibrated ~15 N (1.5 kgf) for 6-7 cm, turning the spring-like sling stop into a near-constant-force stop. Edge and corner landings have 15.7-20 cm of travel and are handled by the sling alone, with folded-newspaper liners on the inside of every edge and corner so no path ends on a skewer. The closed, skinned cube is a drag body (Cd ~1.05, A = 0.070 m^2) that brings a 170 g device to about 6.1 m/s terminal speed within the first 5 m of fall, so a 25 m drop hits no harder than a 2nd-floor drop. The frame and sling are permanent; the cups, corner wraps and film tabs are the sacrificial parts and swap from a spares bag in minutes.

alternatives.name: Balloon-Cage Capsule (air-cushion egg capsule with positively located sponge cradle)
alternatives.concept: A three-stage air-and-foam capsule. Stage 1 (outside): six "balloon pillows", each a free supermarket produce bag holding four soft, deliberately under-inflated 9-inch latex balloons (blown to only about 6 cm, fist-sized, so the latex is barely stretched and does not burst on contact); one pillow is strapped to each face of a 15 cm cardboard cage with rubber bands, and eight small folded-cardboard crumple tubes sit on the cage corners. Stage 2: a 10 cm corrugated core box hangs in the middle of the cage on eight rubber bands (one per corner), with bubble wrap glued to the inside of the cage so the core can never touch bare cardboard when the bands bottom out. Stage 3: inside the core, the egg sits in an egg-shaped pocket cut into a kitchen sponge, with a second sponge on top, so the load is spread over the whole shell. The whole 27 cm cube weighs about 310 g, which gives a terminal velocity of only about 8.3 m/s (reached by the 3rd floor), and about 7.8 cm of soft stopping distance on every face. Because every face carries an identical pillow and every corner a crumple tube, "upside-down" or "sideways" is just another designed landing; the egg can only ever reach latex, plastic, bubble wrap and sponge, never a hard part. The egg comes out through the top lid in under 40 s and goes back into a marked pocket, and the only sacrificial parts (pillows and corner tubes) swap from a bag of pre-made spares in two minutes.

alternatives.name: Stack-Crush Box Mk2 (collar-stabilised layered crumple box)
alternatives.concept: A single-wall cardboard box (26 x 26 x 28 cm) with a flat 2 cm cardboard drag collar around the top rim, so the whole device is 28 x 28 x 28 cm. Inside, from the floor up: a 60 g rice ballast bag, a swappable "cartridge" of 9 inverted paper cups glued under a cardboard plate, a layer of egg-carton cells, then a 14.8 cm cradle box lined with egg-carton pulp in which the egg rides in a marked egg-carton cup glued into a pantyhose pocket that is tensioned to the eight cradle corners by rubber bands. Above the cradle: a second egg-carton layer, a plate and 9 short inverted cups, then the box flaps. Every one of the six faces and all edges/corners has 7 to 9 cm of soft crush path before anything reaches the cradle, and the cradle itself adds 1.75 to 3.75 cm of elastic travel, so the egg can never touch a hard part from any direction. The ballast and heavy bottom cartridge put the centre of mass about 11 cm up; the collar puts the centre of pressure near the top, which biases a base-first landing but is only a bonus. Honest number: a closed box at 0.69 kg only gets to about 11 m/s terminal velocity, so the crush layers, not drag, do the work.

judge_notes.lens: PHYSICS AND SURVIVAL — recomputed v_t, impact speed and peak g from each design's own m, A, Cd and d (rho = 1.2); then re-derived the stopping distance the egg actually experiences after the sling bottoms out, and scored the worst landing orientation (side, edge, corner, inverted, wall clip). Score = P(egg survives 25 m onto concrete in a bad orientation) x 10.
judge_notes.notes: Grafts onto the Hex-Cage (design 2): (1) From the Balloon-Cage, put a 1 cm cellulose sponge disc on the bottom of each of the six cups facing the egg; it spreads the 15-25 N plateau load over the shell and softens the 1.3x buckling spike without changing the calibrated fold force much. (2) From the Balloon-Cage, replace the folded-newspaper corner wraps with 1.5 cm folded-cardboard triangular tubes hot-glued over each corner joint; a corner-first hit puts ~250 N through one hot-glued skewer joint and that is the most likely frame failure. (3) From the Stack-Crush box, back each cup with a full-face cardboard or cereal-box square (not just an 8 cm disc) so a slightly tilted face landing still has the cup bearing on something that reaches the ground, and glue it to the tape diagonals rather than to the film (hot glue melts grocery-bag film). (4) From the Shuttlecock and Lantern, reinforce the eight corner joints with a string or tape lashing before the newspaper or tube goes on, and tie the tethers to the lashing rather than to the glue blob. (5) Buy the energy margin back: the face-on case has ~0 J to spare at 6.1 m/s, so either shave 20-30 g from the frame (every gram lowers v_t^2 proportionally) or double the pantyhose tethers to raise sling stiffness so the egg sheds some speed before it reaches the cup; verify on the 1st-floor calibration drop that cup crush is 3-6 cm. (6) From the Lantern, adopt the pre-departure 1.5 m hand drop onto concrete and the two-hand release 1 m clear of the wall; a wall clip is the one event that pushes the egg through the 1.2 cm packed-cup reserve.

judge_notes.lens: RULES AND BUILDABILITY: each side < 30 cm with margin (nothing protruding), device + egg <= 940 g with the mass budget re-added, a complete materials list obtainable today from home / supermarket / craft / hardware store, buildable in <= 3 h with no power tools, repeatable over 4 drops with cheap pre-cut swaps, every line costed in USD with a total under ~$10, and egg out / back to the same positively-located spot in under a minute.
judge_notes.notes: Grafts for Design 0 (Flat-Top Lantern Lander): (1) From Design 4, pre-build the four bottom crumple cups as one cartridge (cups hot-glued under a single 16 x 16 cm plate at home, plate taped under the sleeve floor with four tape tabs) so the on-site swap is a 1-minute tape job with no glue gun; carry two cartridges. Likewise number the 8 straw-toggle anchors 1-8 so bands always go back to the same holes. (2) From Design 1, drop the egg-carton clamshell (it cannot close over a 6 cm egg with sponge discs) and locate the egg the Shuttlecock way: narrow end on a toe knot, a small band wound twice round the sock neck above the egg, equator marker line on the sock; this also cuts egg-out time to ~30 s and removes a part. Adopt its rule of fixing the sacrificial-part size after the 3rd-floor drop and never changing it. (3) From Design 2, pre-slit and pre-crush the paper cups and do a one-time kitchen-scale fold check on a couple of spares (target ~1.5 kgf) so the cups actually crush at 7 m/s instead of bouncing; keep 20 pre-cut tape tabs stuck to a plastic card for field swaps. (4) From Design 3, duct-tape the sleeve edges and cup-mounting corners so nothing sharp faces the sock, and use its 'trace the egg, mark N' habit on whatever cushion backs the pod. (5) Housekeeping on Design 0's own sheet: inset the four top cups 1 cm from the canopy edge and state it in the materials check; make the sleeve from four separate 16 x 16 panels rather than one 64.8 cm strip so it does not cross a box crease; add double-sided tape (or just tape) as the listed field fastener.

judge_notes.lens: STUDENT DELIVERABLE: can one student sketch it in three dimensioned views, explain the physics to a teacher in two minutes, build it carefully today with few distinct parts, and present/defend it safely on drop day. Rewards clear geometry and an obvious drag -> suspension -> crumple story; penalises hard-to-draw geometry, fiddly calibration, and hand-wavy or self-contradicting numbers.
judge_notes.notes: Graft onto Design 0 (Flat-Top Lantern Lander): (1) From Design 2: cut the rolled rim off every crumple cup, add 3-4 short slits and a 4 mm pre-crush so the cups buckle progressively instead of spiking, and do a one-line kitchen-scale fold check (a cup should fold at roughly 1.3-1.8 kgf) that the student can quote as evidence rather than assumption. (2) From Design 3: cut an egg-shaped pocket into the sponge disc inside the pod (trace the egg, write N at the narrow end) so the egg is located by shape as well as by the pod mark, and write a big TOP arrow on the canopy. (3) From Design 4: number the 8 band anchor holes 1-8 on the sleeve and keep a per-drop log table (floor, landing face, cup heights, pod clearance, swaps, result); keep the device in a plastic bag until the drop so cardboard stays dry. (4) From Design 1: put CoM and CoP marks on the front-view sketch with 'drag' and 'g' arrows and a dimension/volume/mass table beside it; that is the two-minute talk on one page. (5) For the presentation, Design 0 should state a more conservative tolerance line than 90 g (e.g. show margin at 60 g too: designed landing 45 g still passes, corner landing marginal) and keep the second laminated canopy square as a pre-cut spare in case the box is thin. (6) Optionally borrow Design 1's floor-1 attitude check as an explicit pass criterion: spotter confirms canopy-up before any higher drop.

blocking: [Pessimist: worst-case landing orientation (side / edge / corner / inverted / wall clip), real stopping distance the egg gets, and cost / availability] Pillow stage cannot absorb the energy, so the egg breaks on the DESIGNED face landing. The spec needs the four balloons to supply 469 m/s2 x 0.326 kg = 153 N average over 4.5 cm. Four 9-inch balloons inflated to 6 cm (~2x linear stretch, ~3 kPa gauge at best) squashed to a 1.5 cm pancake give ~75 cm2 contact each: 3000 Pa x 0.0075 m2 = 22 N per balloon at END of stroke, ~45 N average for the set, i.e. ~2 J absorbed of the 12 J (spec speed) to 21 J (real speed) arriving. The remaining 10-19 J goes into the single-wall cardboard face hitting concrete through a latex pancake (~1 cm of real crush). The cage stops in ~1 cm at 400+ g; the core closes its 1.1 cm gap at essentially full speed (gap-closure time 9.8 ms vs cage stroke ~4.5 ms) and the egg's true stopping path is bubble wrap 0.7 + the 1 cm pocket floor compressing ~0.6 + lining 0.2 = ~1.5-2.5 cm. a = 8.55^2/(2 x 0.025) = 1460 m/s2 = 149 g average, 224 g at x1.5 peak; at the real 10.2-11.4 m/s it is 265-440 g average. Egg breaks on bottom, top and all four side faces.

[Pessimist: worst-case landing orientation (side / edge / corner / inverted / wall clip), real stopping distance the egg gets, and cost / availability] Peak factor 1.3 is unjustified for three stacked progressive cushions (balloon force ~ contact area ~ x to x^2, bubble wrap pops, sponge densifies). A progressive spring has peak/average >= 2. Even granting the spec's own 7.8 cm and 8.55 m/s: 47.8 g x 2 = 96 g, which is zero margin against its own 100 g assumption and a FAIL (0.73) against the 70 g conservative line the spec itself cites. Safety factor 1.6 is not real.

[Pessimist: worst-case landing orientation (side / edge / corner / inverted / wall clip), real stopping distance the egg gets, and cost / availability] Terminal velocity is understated: four 6 cm balloons in a 2x2 layer cover 12 x 12 cm, not 14 x 14 (you cannot flatten 6 cm spheres to 14 cm and keep 6 cm thickness), so the silhouette is a cross, not a 27 x 27 square: A = (15x15 + 4 x 12x6) = 513 cm2 = 0.0513 m2, not 0.0729. v_t = sqrt(6.396 / (1.2 x Cd x 0.0513)) = 10.2 m/s at Cd 1.0, 11.4 m/s at Cd 0.8 (rounded balloon lobes are plausibly Cd 0.8). KE 17-21 J, i.e. 45-80% more than the 11.9 J designed for. The spec's 'worst case' 9.6 m/s is below its own realistic design speed.

[Pessimist: worst-case landing orientation (side / edge / corner / inverted / wall clip), real stopping distance the egg gets, and cost / availability] Suspension travel is counted as stopping distance but is a free gap. Eight size-32 bands at modest stretch give < 10 N total on the ~130 g core (< 8 g), and the spec's own geometry (15 - 2x0.4 wall - 2x1.0 lining = 12.2 inner, core 10) gives 1.1 cm, not 1.5 cm. Subtracting it from every face path leaves 6.1-7.5 cm even on paper, and the real path per issue 1 is ~2 cm.

[Pessimist: worst-case landing orientation (side / edge / corner / inverted / wall clip), real stopping distance the egg gets, and cost / availability] Edge landing has no crumple element and exposes the taped cardboard edge as the first hard contact. Along the 45-degree edge diagonal the cage edge sits at 10.6 cm from centre, the nearest balloon rim at 13.25 cm: only 2.65 cm of balloon-rim contact at near-zero force before the single-wall cardboard edge hits concrete at 10-11 m/s. Edge crush of single-wall board ~1 cm, core then travels 1.56 cm free diagonally into two bubble-wrapped walls and the egg into a 1.25 cm sponge side wall: ~2 cm real path, 11.4^2 / (2 x 0.02) = 3250 m/s2 = 330 g average. The spec's 59 g for this face is not credible. Corner landing: the corner tube (15.6 cm radius) does take first contact and the cardboard corner crushes 1-2 cm, but the core still arrives at ~10 m/s over ~2.5 cm = 265 g average; also breaks.

[Sceptical physics teacher: recomputed terminal velocity, fall time, impact speed, geometry of the stopping path, series-stage impact dynamics, pillow force capacity, peak factor, and tolerance margin.] Peak factor 1.3 is not conservative for a spring-like stack, and the spec itself calls the stages 'more like a spring than a constant-force crumple'. A linear spring (and any series of linear springs) gives a triangular force profile, peak = 2.0 x average, not 1.3. Using the spec's own distances: face 47.8 g avg -> 96 g peak (margin 1.04, not 1.6); worst-case side at 9.56 m/s, 61.3 g avg -> 123 g peak, which EXCEEDS the 100 g assumption (and the spec's own 70 g cross-check line fails at 0.57). This single correction flips the worst-case verdict from pass to fail.

[Sceptical physics teacher: recomputed terminal velocity, fall time, impact speed, geometry of the stopping path, series-stage impact dynamics, pillow force capacity, peak factor, and tolerance margin.] The 1.5 cm suspension free travel does not exist. Cage inner = 15 - 2 x 0.4 = 14.2 cm; minus 1 cm bubble-wrap lining each side = 12.2 cm clear; core is 10 cm, so free travel is (12.2 - 10)/2 = 1.1 cm per side, and the body-diagonal free travel is 1.1 x sqrt(3) = 1.9 cm, not 2.6 cm. Corrected paths: face 7.4 cm (not 7.8), side 7.2 cm (not 7.6), corner about 6.5 cm (see next item). The sketch guide's '2.5 cm gap = 1 + 1.5' is also wrong: the gap is 2.1 cm.

[Sceptical physics teacher: recomputed terminal velocity, fall time, impact speed, geometry of the stopping path, series-stage impact dynamics, pillow force capacity, peak factor, and tolerance margin.] The stopping distances are summed as if the egg experienced all of them, but the stages are in SERIES behind masses that are only weakly coupled. The core (about 118 g with egg) hangs on 8 size-32 bands that can deliver only a few tens of newtons; while the cage decelerates on the pillow the core keeps its full 8.55 m/s, closes the 1.1 cm gap in about 4 ms, and hits the bubble wrap at essentially full speed when the cage has used only about 2.2 cm of its 4.5 cm pillow stroke (taking cage decel about 1400 m/s2). From that point the egg's remaining decelerating stroke is at most the cage's remaining 2.3 cm of pillow + 0.5 cm bubble wrap + 0.3 cm lining + 1.0 cm sponge = about 4.1 cm, giving 73.1/(2 x 0.041) = 891 m/s2 = 91 g AVERAGE on the egg and about 180 g peak for spring-like stages. The '7.8 cm = sum of stages' model is therefore not physically available to the egg; this is a credible path to a broken egg on the designed face landing, before any worst case.

[Sceptical physics teacher: recomputed terminal velocity, fall time, impact speed, geometry of the stopping path, series-stage impact dynamics, pillow force capacity, peak factor, and tolerance margin.] The balloon pillow has no stated force capacity, and an estimate says it cannot do the job assigned to it. Stopping 11.9 J (0.5 x 0.326 x 8.55^2) in 7.8 cm needs 153 N average on the whole device, and the pillow stage alone has to carry at least that (264 N if it absorbs the energy over its 4.5 cm stroke). Four slack 9-inch balloons at the typical 2-4 kPa gauge pressure of a party balloon, flattened to about 0.03 m2 of footprint, give only 60-120 N, i.e. 1.5-3 J over the last 2.5 cm of stroke; the first 2-3 cm of 'squash' of a barely-inflated balloon is almost force-free because slack latex deforms without compressing the air. Above a few kPa the latex either bursts or the balloons extrude sideways out of the loose produce bag. So most of the 4.5 cm pillow stroke absorbs little energy and the cage arrives at the flat bag with most of its kinetic energy. This is an estimate (no citation), but the spec offers no counter-number and the balloon stage is its biggest single stopping distance.

[Sceptical physics teacher: recomputed terminal velocity, fall time, impact speed, geometry of the stopping path, series-stage impact dynamics, pillow force capacity, peak factor, and tolerance margin.] The corner path of 9.0 cm does not exist. The pillows are 14 x 14 cm on a 15 cm face (an inset of 0.5 cm, not the claimed 0.5 cm overhang; both statements cannot be true), so at a cube corner the first contact is the 3 cm triangular tube, not '3 cm of three pillow corners' plus the tube. Realistic corner path: tube crush 1.5 cm + about 1 cm of glancing pillow edge + 1.9 cm diagonal free travel + 0.9 cm bubble wrap + 1.0 cm sponge = about 6.3-6.5 cm. At 9.56 m/s: 91.4/(2 x 0.065) = 703 m/s2 = 72 g average, 93 g with the spec's own 1.3 factor and 143 g with a spring factor of 2. The spec's corner verdict of 62-78 g rests on distances that are not there.

[Sceptical physics teacher: recomputed terminal velocity, fall time, impact speed, geometry of the stopping path, series-stage impact dynamics, pillow force capacity, peak factor, and tolerance margin.] Tolerance assumption is not conservative in combination with the margins claimed. 100 g peak is at the optimistic end of commonly used rough figures for a raw egg with distributed loading; the spec's own 'conservative' 70 g line already fails its worst case (0.88 by its numbers, 0.57 with a 2x peak factor). A design that only passes at the optimistic tolerance with a 1.3 peak factor is not designed against a conservative assumption.

[Experienced egg-drop maker: buildability in under 3 h with listed materials/tools, step precision, attachment integrity, survival of practice drops, and reusability (egg out/back in under a minute, 4-drop durability, spares and reset)] Egg access cannot be done as written, let alone in 45 s. The core-flap band L3 encircles a 10 cm core that hangs inside a 12.2 cm bubble-wrapped cavity with ~1.1 cm of clearance per side: there is no room to get fingers around the core to slip a band off or back on while the core is suspended on 8 bands. The sponge-sandwich bands L2 have the same problem one level down: the open procedure says 'lift S2 by its notch tab', but S2 is banded to S1 by two bands, and the stack sits snug between W1/W2 inside an 8.6 cm cavity with 0.4 cm total slack, so the whole banded stack has to be prised out of the core before the bands can come off. The real sequence is lid bands, lid, core band (unreachable), flap, W3, pry stack out, two bands off, S2, egg, then all of it in reverse; that is several minutes with the core bouncing on its bands, and it cannot be timed at 45 s. The reusability requirement (egg out in under a minute, back to the identical spot) fails on the procedure, not on the pocket.

[Experienced egg-drop maker: buildability in under 3 h with listed materials/tools, step precision, attachment integrity, survival of practice drops, and reusability (egg out/back in under a minute, 4-drop durability, spares and reset)] Corner crumple tube attachment will fail on the first hit. Step 5 says to hot-glue an equilateral triangular prism 'so one flat side sits on the corner': a 3 x 4 cm flat face laid against a cube vertex touches the cube at a single point, so the tube is held by a blob of glue bridging three faces at a point and will shear off on a corner or edge strike, exactly when it is needed. With the pillows at 12 cm actual footprint (see next item) the cardboard corner is the first thing to touch concrete on a corner landing, so the only corner protection is this glued-on tube.

[Experienced egg-drop maker: buildability in under 3 h with listed materials/tools, step precision, attachment integrity, survival of practice drops, and reusability (egg out/back in under a minute, 4-drop durability, spares and reset)] Pillow geometry is inconsistent and leaves edges and corners far less protected than claimed, so the practice-drop survival numbers are wrong. Four 6 cm balloons in a 2 x 2 layer give a 12 x 12 cm footprint, not 14 x 14, and a 14 cm pillow cannot 'overhang the cage edges by 0.5 cm' on a 15 cm face anyway. Recomputed with balloon centres 3 cm off the face and 3 cm from the centreline: on an edge-first landing the balloons protrude only 1.9 cm past the duct-taped cardboard edge (spec claims 4 cm of squash), and the corner tubes are only 4 cm long on a 15 cm edge, so the middle 7 cm of every edge hits concrete after ~2 cm. Edge stopping distance is ~5.8 cm, not 8.8: 90 g at 8.55 m/s and ~112 g at the 9.6 m/s worst case, over the 100 g design line. On a corner landing the balloon surfaces sit 0.5 cm INSIDE the cage corner along the body diagonal, so the claimed '3 cm of pillow corners' does not exist; corner d is ~7.5 cm and ~93 g at 9.6 m/s, marginal. A tumbling cube landing edge-first on the 3rd-floor practice drop is a likely crack.

[Experienced egg-drop maker: buildability in under 3 h with listed materials/tools, step precision, attachment integrity, survival of practice drops, and reusability (egg out/back in under a minute, 4-drop durability, spares and reset)] The 170-minute schedule has zero margin and the two longest steps are understated, so the build does not fit 3 h. Step 1 allots 15 min to lay out and cut 28 pieces (six 15 cm squares, six 10 cm squares, sixteen 4 x 9 cm strips) from 3-4 mm corrugated with two box-cutter passes per cut: that is 100+ cuts and realistically 25-35 min. Step 6 allots 20 min to carve a 1.5 cm deep egg-shaped recess (not a through cut) into a dry cellulose sponge with scissors, in 2 mm enlargement steps, plus a dimple in a second sponge; scissors cannot gouge a blind pocket in dry cellulose, it needs a damp sponge and a box cutter, and is a 30 min job for a first-timer. Add glue-gun warm-up, 32 balloons inflated by mouth, and the 1 m bench-drop series, and the realistic total is 3.5-4 h.

[Experienced egg-drop maker: buildability in under 3 h with listed materials/tools, step precision, attachment integrity, survival of practice drops, and reusability (egg out/back in under a minute, 4-drop durability, spares and reset)] Suspension as specified has no tension. A size 32 band (7.6 cm flat, 15.2 cm loop) lark's-headed through a core hole hangs as a ~3.8 cm doubled loop, but the core-corner-to-anchor distance is only 2.8 cm (sqrt(3 x 1.6^2)), so every band is slack by ~1 cm and the core rests on the floor bubble wrap instead of floating; the spec's own 'stretched to about 2.5 cm' and 'stretched 1.3x at rest' are contradictory. Step 7's tip (wrap once more around the straw) is the actual build method, and must be applied to all 8 bands, but it is written as an optional fix, so a student following the steps gets a core that does not 'spring back to centre' and the push test in the protocol fails.
non_blocking: [Pessimist: worst-case landing orientation (side / edge / corner / inverted / wall clip), real stopping distance the egg gets, and cost / availability] Cost passes: 5.90 USD as written; worst case with duct tape and bubble wrap bought adds 2.50 = 8.40 USD, still under 10. Egg line (3 for 0.90) is optimistic for 2026 US prices; budget ~1.50. Nothing exotic; everything is dollar-store/supermarket. Mass budget adds to 326 g; 27 cm per side passes (would actually be ~25-27 cm given 12 cm balloon footprints).

[Pessimist: worst-case landing orientation (side / edge / corner / inverted / wall clip), real stopping distance the egg gets, and cost / availability] Sponge numbers: the pocket floor is only 1 cm thick (2.5 cm sponge, 1.5 cm pocket) and cannot 'compress 1.0 cm'; dry cellulose densifies at ~60-70% strain, so ~0.6 cm. The 1.25 cm sponge wall beside the egg on side landings is even thinner. The top (S2) path is actually better than the bottom (2 cm above the dimple).

[Pessimist: worst-case landing orientation (side / edge / corner / inverted / wall clip), real stopping distance the egg gets, and cost / availability] Local hard points inside the core: the 8 lark's-head band loops sit inside the core box at the corners under the 0.3 cm lining; after the sponge densifies, a side or corner hit loads the sponge corner onto a band knot and hole edge. Egg is ~3 cm from them, so not direct contact, but the 'no hard part inside the core' claim is overstated.

[Pessimist: worst-case landing orientation (side / edge / corner / inverted / wall clip), real stopping distance the egg gets, and cost / availability] Pillow description inconsistent: 'flatten each pillow to 14 x 14 x 6' is impossible with four 6 cm balloons; pillows are 12 x 12 x 6 and adjacent pillows do not meet at the edges as claimed (bottom pillow ends at x = 6, side pillow starts at x = 7.5).

[Pessimist: worst-case landing orientation (side / edge / corner / inverted / wall clip), real stopping distance the egg gets, and cost / availability] Reusability: egg access in ~45 s via lid, core flap, S2 is plausible and the traced pocket plus N mark is a genuine positive locator. Spares are tight: at the real impact speeds expect the landing-face balloons to burst every drop; 2 built pillows + 2 field-made covers exactly 4 drops with no slack.

[Pessimist: worst-case landing orientation (side / edge / corner / inverted / wall clip), real stopping distance the egg gets, and cost / availability] Honest aspects worth keeping if redesigned: the symmetric cube with every face identical, the numbered anchors, the pre-cut tape card, the test ladder and the 2 m corner-first bench drop. The fix is not more balloons but a real crush stage on the cage (e.g. 6-8 cm of stacked corrugated honeycomb or paper-cup/egg-carton crumple on every face) and a compliant, not slack, suspension.

[Sceptical physics teacher: recomputed terminal velocity, fall time, impact speed, geometry of the stopping path, series-stage impact dynamics, pillow force capacity, peak factor, and tolerance margin.] Drag numbers check out: with m = 0.326 kg, A = 0.0729 m2, Cd = 1.0, rho = 1.2: v_t = 8.55 m/s; numeric integration of m dv/dt = mg - 0.5 rho Cd A v^2 gives 6.67 m/s at 3.5 m, 8.29 m/s at 10.5 m, 8.51 m/s at 17.5 m, 8.55 m/s at 25 m, fall time 3.53 s; Cd = 0.8 gives 9.54 m/s and 3.29 s. Ladder speeds and the 2.3 s no-drag time are right. Cd = 1.0 for a soft-faced cube is a reasonable, slightly conservative pick; Cd = 0.8 sensitivity is sensible.

[Sceptical physics teacher: recomputed terminal velocity, fall time, impact speed, geometry of the stopping path, series-stage impact dynamics, pillow force capacity, peak factor, and tolerance margin.] Mass budget sums to 326 g and cost to 5.90 USD; cardboard mass (0.135 m2 x 450 g/m2 = 61 g) and balloon mass are plausible. Both limits (27 cm < 30 cm, 326 g < 940 g) are met with margin.

Eight size-32 bands at modest stretch give < 10 N total on the ~130 g core (< 8 g), and the spec's own geometry (15 - 2x0.4 wall - 2x1.0 lining = 12.2 inner, core 10) gives 1.1 cm, not 1.5 cm. Subtracting it from every face path leaves 6.1-7.5 cm even on paper, and the real path per issue 1 is ~2 cm.

Along the 45-degree edge diagonal the cage edge sits at 10.6 cm from centre, the nearest balloon rim at 13.25 cm: only 2.65 cm of balloon-rim contact at near-zero force before the single-wall cardboard edge hits concrete at 10-11 m/s. Edge crush of single-wall board ~1 cm, core then travels 1.56 cm free diagonally into two bubble-wrapped walls and the egg into a 1.25 cm sponge side wall: ~2 cm real path, 11.4^2 / (2 x 0.02) = 3250 m/s2 = 330 g average. The spec's 59 g for this face is not credible. Corner landing: the corner tube (15.6 cm radius) does take first contact and the cardboard corner crushes 1-2 cm, but the core still arrives at ~10 m/s over ~2.5 cm = 265 g average; also breaks.

[Sceptical physics teacher: recomputed terminal velocity, fall time, impact speed, geometry of the stopping path, series-stage impact dynamics, pillow force capacity, peak factor, and tolerance margin.] Peak factor 1.3 is not conservative for a spring-like stack, and the spec itself calls the stages 'more like a spring than a constant-force crumple'. A linear spring (and any series of linear springs) gives a triangular force profile, peak = 2.0 x average, not 1.3. Using the spec's own distances: face 47.8 g avg -> 96 g peak (margin 1.04, not 1.6); worst-case side at 9.56 m/s, 61.3 g avg -> 123 g peak, which EXCEEDS the 100 g assumption (and the spec's own 70 g cross-check line fails at 0.57). This single correction flips the worst-case verdict from pass to fail.

[Sceptical physics teacher: recomputed terminal velocity, fall time, impact speed, geometry of the stopping path, series-stage impact dynamics, pillow force capacity, peak factor, and tolerance margin.] The 1.5 cm suspension free travel does not exist. Cage inner = 15 - 2 x 0.4 = 14.2 cm; minus 1 cm bubble-wrap lining each side = 12.2 cm clear; core is 10 cm, so free travel is (12.2 - 10)/2 = 1.1 cm per side, and the body-diagonal free travel is 1.1 x sqrt(3) = 1.9 cm, not 2.6 cm. Corrected paths: face 7.4 cm (not 7.8), side 7.2 cm (not 7.6), corner about 6.5 cm (see next item). The sketch guide's '2.5 cm gap = 1 + 1.5' is also wrong: the gap is 2.1 cm.

[Sceptical physics teacher: recomputed terminal velocity, fall time, impact speed, geometry of the stopping path, series-stage impact dynamics, pillow force capacity, peak factor, and tolerance margin.] The stopping distances are summed as if the egg experienced all of them, but the stages are in SERIES behind masses that are only weakly coupled. The core (about 118 g with egg) hangs on 8 size-32 bands that can deliver only a few tens of newtons; while the cage decelerates on the pillow the core keeps its full 8.55 m/s, closes the 1.1 cm gap in about 4 ms, and hits the bubble wrap at essentially full speed when the cage has used only about 2.2 cm of its 4.5 cm pillow stroke (taking cage decel about 1400 m/s2). From that point the egg's remaining decelerating stroke is at most the cage's remaining 2.3 cm of pillow + 0.5 cm bubble wrap + 0.3 cm lining + 1.0 cm sponge = about 4.1 cm, giving 73.1/(2 x 0.041) = 891 m/s2 = 91 g AVERAGE on the egg and about 180 g peak for spring-like stages. The '7.8 cm = sum of stages' model is therefore not physically available to the egg; this is a credible path to a broken egg on the designed face landing, before any worst case.

[Sceptical physics teacher: recomputed terminal velocity, fall time, impact speed, geometry of the stopping path, series-stage impact dynamics, pillow force capacity, peak factor, and tolerance margin.] The balloon pillow has no stated force capacity, and an estimate says it cannot do the job assigned to it. Stopping 11.9 J (0.5 x 0.326 x 8.55^2) in 7.8 cm needs 153 N average on the whole device, and the pillow stage alone has to carry at least that (264 N if it absorbs the energy over its 4.5 cm stroke). Four slack 9-inch balloons at the typical 2-4 kPa gauge pressure of a party balloon, flattened to about 0.03 m2 of footprint, give only 60-120 N, i.e. 1.5-3 J over the last 2.5 cm of stroke; the first 2-3 cm of 'squash' of a barely-inflated balloon is almost force-free because slack latex deforms without compressing the air. Above a few kPa the latex either bursts or the balloons extrude sideways out of the loose produce bag. So most of the 4.5 cm pillow stroke absorbs little energy and the cage arrives at the flat bag with most of its kinetic energy. This is an estimate (no citation), but the spec offers no counter-number and the balloon stage is its biggest single stopping distance.

[Sceptical physics teacher: recomputed terminal velocity, fall time, impact speed, geometry of the stopping path, series-stage impact dynamics, pillow force capacity, peak factor, and tolerance margin.] The corner path of 9.0 cm does not exist. The pillows are 14 x 14 cm on a 15 cm face (an inset of 0.5 cm, not the claimed 0.5 cm overhang; both statements cannot be true), so at a cube corner the first contact is the 3 cm triangular tube, not '3 cm of three pillow corners' plus the tube. Realistic corner path: tube crush 1.5 cm + about 1 cm of glancing pillow edge + 1.9 cm diagonal free travel + 0.9 cm bubble wrap + 1.0 cm sponge = about 6.3-6.5 cm. At 9.56 m/s: 91.4/(2 x 0.065) = 703 m/s2 = 72 g average, 93 g with the spec's own 1.3 factor and 143 g with a spring factor of 2. The spec's corner verdict of 62-78 g rests on distances that are not there.

[Sceptical physics teacher: recomputed terminal velocity, fall time, impact speed, geometry of the stopping path, series-stage impact dynamics, pillow force capacity, peak factor, and tolerance margin.] Tolerance assumption is not conservative in combination with the margins claimed. 100 g peak is at the optimistic end of commonly used rough figures for a raw egg with distributed loading; the spec's own 'conservative' 70 g line already fails its worst case (0.88 by its numbers, 0.57 with a 2x peak factor). A design that only passes at the optimistic tolerance with a 1.3 peak factor is not designed against a conservative assumption.

[Experienced egg-drop maker: buildability in under 3 h with listed materials/tools, step precision, attachment integrity, survival of practice drops, and reusability (egg out/back in under a minute, 4-drop durability, spares and reset)] Egg access cannot be done as written, let alone in 45 s. The core-flap band L3 encircles a 10 cm core that hangs inside a 12.2 cm bubble-wrapped cavity with ~1.1 cm of clearance per side: there is no room to get fingers around the core to slip a band off or back on while the core is suspended on 8 bands. The sponge-sandwich bands L2 have the same problem one level down: the open procedure says 'lift S2 by its notch tab', but S2 is banded to S1 by two bands, and the stack sits snug between W1/W2 inside an 8.6 cm cavity with 0.4 cm total slack, so the whole banded stack has to be prised out of the core before the bands can come off. The real sequence is lid bands, lid, core band (unreachable), flap, W3, pry stack out, two bands off, S2, egg, then all of it in reverse; that is several minutes with the core bouncing on its bands, and it cannot be timed at 45 s. The reusability requirement (egg out in under a minute, back to the identical spot) fails on the procedure, not on the pocket.

[Experienced egg-drop maker: buildability in under 3 h with listed materials/tools, step precision, attachment integrity, survival of practice drops, and reusability (egg out/back in under a minute, 4-drop durability, spares and reset)] Corner crumple tube attachment will fail on the first hit. Step 5 says to hot-glue an equilateral triangular prism 'so one flat side sits on the corner': a 3 x 4 cm flat face laid against a cube vertex touches the cube at a single point, so the tube is held by a blob of glue bridging three faces at a point and will shear off on a corner or edge strike, exactly when it is needed. With the pillows at 12 cm actual footprint (see next item) the cardboard corner is the first thing to touch concrete on a corner landing, so the only corner protection is this glued-on tube.

[Experienced egg-drop maker: buildability in under 3 h with listed materials/tools, step precision, attachment integrity, survival of practice drops, and reusability (egg out/back in under a minute, 4-drop durability, spares and reset)] Pillow geometry is inconsistent and leaves edges and corners far less protected than claimed, so the practice-drop survival numbers are wrong. Four 6 cm balloons in a 2 x 2 layer give a 12 x 12 cm footprint, not 14 x 14, and a 14 cm pillow cannot 'overhang the cage edges by 0.5 cm' on a 15 cm face anyway. Recomputed with balloon centres 3 cm off the face and 3 cm from the centreline: on an edge-first landing the balloons protrude only 1.9 cm past the duct-taped cardboard edge (spec claims 4 cm of squash), and the corner tubes are only 4 cm long on a 15 cm edge, so the middle 7 cm of every edge hits concrete after ~2 cm. Edge stopping distance is ~5.8 cm, not 8.8: 90 g at 8.55 m/s and ~112 g at the 9.6 m/s worst case, over the 100 g design line. On a corner landing the balloon surfaces sit 0.5 cm INSIDE the cage corner along the body diagonal, so the claimed '3 cm of pillow corners' does not exist; corner d is ~7.5 cm and ~93 g at 9.6 m/s, marginal. A tumbling cube landing edge-first on the 3rd-floor practice drop is a likely crack.

[Experienced egg-drop maker: buildability in under 3 h with listed materials/tools, step precision, attachment integrity, survival of practice drops, and reusability (egg out/back in under a minute, 4-drop durability, spares and reset)] The 170-minute schedule has zero margin and the two longest steps are understated, so the build does not fit 3 h. Step 1 allots 15 min to lay out and cut 28 pieces (six 15 cm squares, six 10 cm squares, sixteen 4 x 9 cm strips) from 3-4 mm corrugated with two box-cutter passes per cut: that is 100+ cuts and realistically 25-35 min. Step 6 allots 20 min to carve a 1.5 cm deep egg-shaped recess (not a through cut) into a dry cellulose sponge with scissors, in 2 mm enlargement steps, plus a dimple in a second sponge; scissors cannot gouge a blind pocket in dry cellulose, it needs a damp sponge and a box cutter, and is a 30 min job for a first-timer. Add glue-gun warm-up, 32 balloons inflated by mouth, and the 1 m bench-drop series, and the realistic total is 3.5-4 h.

[Experienced egg-drop maker: buildability in under 3 h with listed materials/tools, step precision, attachment integrity, survival of practice drops, and reusability (egg out/back in under a minute, 4-drop durability, spares and reset)] Suspension as specified has no tension. A size 32 band (7.6 cm flat, 15.2 cm loop) lark's-headed through a core hole hangs as a ~3.8 cm doubled loop, but the core-corner-to-anchor distance is only 2.8 cm (sqrt(3 x 1.6^2)), so every band is slack by ~1 cm and the core rests on the floor bubble wrap instead of floating; the spec's own 'stretched to about 2.5 cm' and 'stretched 1.3x at rest' are contradictory. Step 7's tip (wrap once more around the straw) is the actual build method, and must be applied to all 8 bands, but it is written as an optional fix, so a student following the steps gets a core that does not 'spring back to centre' and the push test in the protocol fails.
